name: Ananiah
title: Co-signer of the Covenant
summary: Ananiah was among the elected leaders who sealed the solemn covenant with God during the great religious renewal in Jerusalem after returning from Babylon. In connection with Nehemiah's reforms and Ezra's reading of the law, the Jewish community experienced a deep spiritual revival that culminated in a written covenant. Ananiah committed himself, along with other leaders, priests, and Levites, to faithful obedience to the Mosaic Law. The covenant included promises to keep the Sabbath holy, preserve the people's identity through marriage practices, and faithfully support temple service. A person with the same name is also mentioned among those who stood beside Ezra during the solemn reading of the law at the Water Gate, but it is uncertain whether this is the same individual.

keyEvents.title: The Sealing of the Covenant
keyEvents.description: Ananiah was among the people's leaders who placed their seal on the covenant to follow God's law, as it was read aloud by Ezra and explained by the Levites.

keyEvents.title: The People's Commitment to the Law
keyEvents.description: Together with other leaders, Ananiah committed himself to walk in God's law given through Moses, God's servant, and to keep all the Lord's commands and regulations.

keyEvents.title: Possible Participation at Ezra's Reading of the Law
keyEvents.description: A man named Ananiah stood at Ezra's right hand as he read the law aloud to the people by the Water Gate. It is debated whether this is the same Ananiah who sealed the covenant.

keyEvents.title: The People's Confession and Covenant Making
keyEvents.description: The people gathered for fasting and confession of sin, with the Levites leading in praise and prayer to God. This formed the background for the covenant making in which Ananiah participated.

versions.summary: Anajah was one of the leaders among the people who placed their seal on the covenant with God in Nehemiah's time. He is mentioned in connection with the renewal of the covenant after Israel's return from the Babylonian exile. He was among the Israelites who committed themselves to follow God's law.
versions.title: Co-signer of the Covenant
versions.reason: [major] Ananiah is mentioned in Nehemiah 10:22 in some translations, but in the Hebrew text, Ananiah is named in Neh 10:23 among the people's leaders who sealed the covenant. Verse numbering may vary, so this should be verified. In many Norwegian translations, Ananiah is actually listed in Neh 10:22 among the heads of the people, so this can be accepted; however, it is important to note that the numbering in the Hebrew text differs by one verse (Neh 10:1 in Norwegian translations = Neh 10:2 in Hebrew).; [major] There is no evidence that Ananiah was present at Ezra's reading of the Law in Nehemiah 8:1-3. Neh 8:4 mentions a person named Ananiah (or similar) who stood beside Ezra during the reading of the Law, but this may be another individual. The event should still be checked: In Neh 8:4, people are mentioned standing beside Ezra, and Ananiah is among them. This could be the same person, but it remains uncertain. The description should be clarified to refer specifically to Neh 8:4 if this event is included.; [major] If Ananiah is mentioned in connection with Ezra's reading of the Law, the relevant reference is Nehemiah 8:4, not 8:1-3. Verses 1-3 describe the reading of the Law generally, while verse 4 names those who stood beside Ezra. The reference should be updated to include verse 4.; [minor] Neh 9:1-3 and 9:38 describe the people's confession and covenant-making in general terms, but Ananiah is not specifically named in this chapter. This provides reasonable context, but it should be clarified that this serves as background for the covenant-making rather than an event where Ananiah is directly named.; [minor] The role "leader" is appropriate but somewhat general. It may be worth adding "co-sealer of the covenant" or "people's leader" to specify his role more precisely.; [minor] The summary is good, but the profile could be enriched by noting that a person named Ananiah possibly also stood beside Ezra during the reading of the Law (Neh 8:4), even though it is unclear whether this is the same individual.; [minor] The profile lacks footnotes. Notes should be added regarding the meaning of the name, the historical context, and possibly the question of whether the Ananiah in Neh 8:4 and Neh 10:22 is the same person.

versions.summary: Ananiah was one of the people's leaders who set his seal on the covenant with God during the great renewal in Nehemiah's time. After returning from the Babylonian exile, the Jewish community in Jerusalem underwent a comprehensive religious reform process led by Nehemiah and Ezra. As part of this renewal, Ananiah committed himself, along with other leaders, to follow God's law as given through Moses. The covenant included promises such as keeping the Sabbath holy, remaining faithful to the people's identity in marriage, and supporting temple service. A person with the same name is also mentioned among those who stood beside Ezra during the solemn reading of the Law at the Water Gate, but it is uncertain whether this is the same individual.

Given that the profile already discusses this in a footnote, it is acceptable to keep verse 22, but consideration should be given to whether verse 23 should also be included for completeness.; [minor] The summary is well phrased and covers the main points well. A slightly different introduction could have been advantageous to distinguish it more clearly from earlier versions.; [minor] The role 'co-sealer of the covenant' partially overlaps with the title. It might have been more precise to use a role such as 'covenant signatory' or similar to avoid repeating the title.

footnotes.text: The name Anajah (Hebrew: עֲנָיָה, 'Anayah') likely means "the Lord has answered" or "Yahweh has responded," composed of the Hebrew verb 'anah' (to answer) and the shortened divine name form '-yah'. This type of theophoric name was very common in the post-Babylonian period and expresses the parents' gratitude to God.

There may be two people named Anajah in the book of Nehemiah: one who stood beside Ezra during the reading of the Law (Neh 8:4) and one who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:22–23). Many scholars consider it likely that these are two different individuals, since one appears to have had a more prominent role in the reading of the Law, possibly a priest or Levite, while the other is listed among the heads of the people.

The covenant-making in Nehemiah 10 took place after Israel's return from the Babylonian exile, probably around 445–444 BC during Nehemiah's governorship. The covenant included commitments to keep the Sabbath, not to marry foreign peoples, and to support temple service through tithes and offerings.

The verse numbering in Nehemiah 10 varies between the Hebrew Masoretic text and different translations. In the Hebrew text, what is counted as verse 1 in some translations is regarded as the last verse of chapter 9 in the Masoretic tradition, resulting in a one-verse shift throughout the chapter.

The sealing of the covenant in Nehemiah 10 represents an important example of collective religious commitment in post-Babylonian Israel. The list of signatories is arranged in three groups: priests, Levites, and heads of the people, reflecting the social structure of the restored Jewish community in the province of Yehud under Persian rule.
